explain.say: A hot cup of chai on the table always cools down; it never gets hotter by drawing heat from the cooler room. Energy would be conserved either way, so the first law cannot explain this. We need a second law. In 1865 Rudolf Clausius named the quantity that decides: entropy. Look at heat flowing from hot to cold.

draw.text: Heat flows by itself only from hot to cold

explain.say: Entropy is a measure of how spread out energy is. Watch the particles mix: they spread out by themselves and never gather back on their own. Energy behaves the same way. The second law says the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Have you ever seen spilled milk unmix?

draw.text: Second law: ΔS_total ≥ 0 for an isolated system

explain.say: Never! Let us measure it. For heat Q at temperature T, the entropy change is Q over T. Let 1000 kilojoules flow from 500 kelvin to 300 kelvin. The hot side loses 1000 over 500, which is 2 kilojoules per kelvin. The cold side gains 1000 over 300, about 3.33. See the two bars? Is the total up or down?

Up, by 1.33 kilojoules per kelvin, so the flow happens by itself. Run it backwards and the total would fall, which is forbidden. The same law limits engines: the Kelvin–Planck statement says no engine can turn all its heat into work. Some must be dumped to a cold sink. See the engine, with heat out at the bottom?

explain.say: That waste heat is why power stations have cooling towers. Fantastic work! Exam tip: entropy change Q over T is exact only for reversible heat transfer; real processes always create extra entropy. Wow fact: entropy is the reason time seems to have a direction. Challenge: what is the entropy change if the cold side were 400 kelvin?

faq.q: Why does heat flow from hot to cold?
faq.a: Heat flowing from hot to cold increases the total entropy, because the cold body gains more entropy than the hot body loses. The reverse would decrease entropy, which the second law forbids without outside work.
asks: why does heat not flow from cold to hot

faq.q: What is entropy in simple words?
faq.a: Entropy measures how spread out, or disordered, energy is. Left alone, energy spreads out, so the entropy of an isolated system rises or stays the same.

faq.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics say?
faq.a: The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Equivalent forms: heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself (Clausius), and no engine turns all its heat into work (Kelvin–Planck).

faq.q: Why can no engine turn all its heat into work?
faq.a: Taking heat from a hot source lowers its entropy. To keep the total entropy from falling, the engine must dump some heat into a cold sink, raising the sink's entropy.

faq.q: How do I calculate entropy change for heat transfer?
faq.a: For heat Q at a constant temperature T in kelvin, the entropy change is Q over T. Add the changes for every body involved to get the total.
asks: entropy change formula Q over T

facts: Rudolf Clausius introduced the word entropy in 1865.
For reversible heat transfer at constant temperature, the entropy change is Q divided by the absolute temperature.

wrong.1: That has the signs swapped; the hot body loses entropy and the cold one gains more.
